title: The Secret Language of Old-Growth Forests
content:
Walk into an old-growth forest and you step into a conversation that has been going on for centuries. Beneath the leaf litter, a vast web of fungal threads connects tree to tree, carrying sugars, water, and warning signals between the tallest canopy giants and the youngest seedlings on the forest floor. Foresters have taken to calling it the wood wide web, and it upends the old idea of the forest as a crowd of solitary trees competing for light.

A mother tree, the oldest and largest in a stand, can be linked to hundreds of its neighbours. When a seedling is struggling in deep shade, sugars flow toward it through the network. When one tree comes under attack from insects, chemical alarms travel through the soil and neighbouring trees begin to raise their defences before the pests even arrive. Cut the connections, and the whole community grows more slowly and more sickly. It turns out a forest is less a collection of individuals than a single, patient, living thing that measures its life in centuries.
featured_text: Beneath every ancient forest runs a hidden network of fungi and roots, quietly sharing food and sending warnings between the trees. It is one of nature's oldest conversations.

title: Following the Autumn Migration
content:
Each autumn, as the light softens and the first cold nights arrive, something ancient stirs in millions of birds. Almost overnight the skies fill with movement as swallows, warblers, and geese begin the long journey south. Some will cross entire oceans without landing, navigating by the stars, the setting sun, and a magnetic sense we are only beginning to understand.

Standing on a headland at first light during the migration is one of nature's great free spectacles. Waves of small birds pour overhead, pausing in the hedgerows to feed before pressing on. A single willow warbler weighing less than a two-pound coin may travel from a northern woodland all the way to sub-Saharan Africa and back again the following spring, guided home to the very same tree it left. The more we learn about these journeys, the more astonishing it becomes that creatures so small carry maps so vast inside them.
featured_text: As the nights draw in, millions of birds set out on journeys that span oceans and continents, navigating by the stars to reach places they have never seen and return home again.
